chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

He (peace be upon him) said to me: 'What withheld you from the Hajj?' I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you! A great debt fell upon me, and my wealth is gone, and the debt that has become obligatory upon me is greater than the wealth that has gone. So if a man from our companions had not paid it for me, I would not have been able to go out.' So he (peace be upon him) said to me: 'If you are patient, you will be glad (of the reward), and if you are not patient, Allah will implement His decree, whether you are pleased with it or reluctant.'

key_terms.أَخْرَجَنِي: paid my debt / took me out
key_terms.تُغْتَبَطْ: you will be glad / receive glad tidings
key_terms.رَاضِياً كُنْتَ أَمْ كَارِهاً: whether you are pleased or reluctant

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for patiently enduring debt and financial hardship according to Imam al-Rida?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) addresses Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who missed Hajj due to overwhelming debt that exceeded his lost wealth, a burden alleviated only by a companion's intervention. The Imam’s teaching underscores the Shia concept of 'Sabr' (patience) not merely as passive endurance but as an active spiritual state that invites divine gladness (ughtabat), contrasting it with the inevitability of Allah's decree (maqadir) which unfolds whether one is content or resentful. This highlights the theological balance between human effort in resolving obligations and submission to divine will during periods of financial trial.
